message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
Here's everything, starting with tomorrow's route since that's the time-critical one.

## Tomorrow's route: B → A → C

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at B (20 min drive) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B ✅ done before the shop opens at 09:30 |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive B → A (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A ✅ within the 09:00–10:00 window |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive A → C (40 min) |
| 10:25–11:00 | **Wait at C; take the 30-minute break here** |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at C ✅ not before 11:00 |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive C → depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | Back at depot ✅, just in time |

**Why this is the only order that works:**
- B has to come first. Starting at A means arriving at 09:00 at the earliest, finishing at 09:15, and reaching B at 09:40, after the shop opens.
- C has to come last, because it can't take anything before 11:00, which is after A's window closes.
- The 35-minute wait at C is where the break fits, so it costs no extra time.

**⚠️ The return has zero slack.** C can't start before 11:00, then unloading takes 15 minutes and the drive back takes 45, so 12:00 is the earliest possible return regardless of anything else. Any delay at C, such as a late handover, a tricky carry or traffic, makes the van late back. It's worth doing one of these:
- Confirming tonight that C will be ready to receive at 11:00 sharp, with someone waiting and a clear route in.
- Checking whether the 12:00 return has any flexibility.
- Warning whoever is waiting for the van at noon that it may be a few minutes late.

The morning is easier: there's 25 minutes of spare time at B and 15 at A.

## Names for the van

- **Dovetail**
- **The Chiffonier**
- **Van Gogh**
- **French Polish**
- **Sir Lifts-a-Lot**
- **The Restoration Wagon**

Dovetail suits a furniture restorer best. Van Gogh will probably win the vote.

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> "Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Company]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!"

## Three checks before handing furniture over

1. **Condition.** Check for new scratches, dents or knocks picked up in transit. Comparing with photos taken at loading is the best way.
2. **Moving parts.** Make sure doors, drawers, hinges, locks and castors open, close and run smoothly.
3. **Everything's there and secure.** Check for all keys, handles, shelves, feet and fittings, and make sure the piece stands level and stable.

If there's a problem, note it and photograph it before the customer signs.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Email by default.** It's easier to store, search and resend, and it can't get lost in the van. Have customers sign on a phone or tablet, and email the signed note automatically. Keep a paper option for customers who prefer it or don't use email.

## Proof of delivery, in one line

**"Proof of delivery is the signed and dated record, usually with a photo, showing the item was delivered to the right person, in good condition, at a stated time."**

## Evening-before text (under 160 characters)

> "Hi [Name], it's [Company]. Your furniture is due tomorrow between [9:00] and [10:00]. Any problem, call [number]. Thanks!"

With a typical name, company and phone number filled in, this comes to about **130 characters**. For example, "Hi Sarah, it's Oakwood Restoration. Your furniture is due tomorrow between 9:00 and 10:00. Any problem, call 01234 567890. Thanks!" is 130.

**One trap to watch:** emoji, curly apostrophes (’) or curly quotation marks in a text switch it to a different encoding with a limit of **70 characters**. Your message would then be split into two or three texts. Use a straight apostrophe (') in "it's" and leave out emoji. Some systems convert apostrophes automatically, so send yourself a test first.
